fields.meta_title: Low Stock Alert Rules That Reach the Right Person | Emergent
fields.meta_description: See a low stock alert built four ways: item thresholds, sales speed against lead time, store counts, and escalation when nobody acts.
fields.h1: Build a Low Stock Alert That Reaches the Right Person
fields.hero_description: Build a low stock alert that tells the person who restocks each item, while there is still time to order.
fields.features_heading: What Emergent Builds Into a Stock Alert App
fields.features_subheading: Each item gets its own rule and its own owner, and every alert stays on record until someone acts on it.
fields.feature_1:
Rules you write in a sentence

Type the rule as you would tell a new buyer: alert me when the kettle drops under 15. Emergent builds the app, its database, and the logic, and a new prompt changes the number.
fields.feature_2:
Counts from the systems you sell through

The app connects to any tool with an API, so counts can come in from your point of sale, online store, or warehouse system. Each sale or receipt moves the count it checks.
fields.feature_3:
One owner for every alert

Each alert goes to the person who restocks that item, by Slack, email, or in the app. A reminder follows if it sits untouched, then an escalation to the next person you name.
fields.feature_4:
Thresholds that follow sales speed

A fixed number suits slow sellers. For fast ones, the app divides units on hand by daily sales and compares the result with the supplier's lead time, so a busy week alerts sooner.
fields.feature_5:
A live board of items under threshold

A dashboard lists each item below its line, its owner, and whether it is marked ordered. It updates in real time as counts change, and alert history sits in a database you own.
fields.feature_6:
No cap when the checks pile up

Busy holiday weeks run more checks, with no task cap to hit. Paid plans export the full code to your GitHub repository, and the free tier covers building and publishing.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Low Stock Alerts at One Shop
fields.tab_content_1:
The kettle drops to 12 units, under its threshold of 15

At 10:40 a.m., a sale takes the 1.2-liter pour-over kettle at Corvina Home Goods to 12 units, under the threshold of 15 the buyer set. The app sends the buyer, Ezinne Fairweather-Kim, an in-app alert with the count against the threshold and a Mark ordered button. Once she taps it, the board shows the kettle as Ordered.
fields.tab_content_2:
9 days of cover against a 10-day lead time sends the alert

Linen napkin sets sell 6 a day at Corvina Home Goods, and the supplier needs 10 days to deliver. With 54 sets left, the app counts 9 days of cover, 1 day short of the lead time, and emails Ezinne Fairweather-Kim. The fixed threshold of 25 sets is still far off.
fields.tab_content_3:
With 140 mugs in the warehouse, Kestrel Lane has 3

The Kestrel Lane store is down to 3 stoneware mugs, under its store threshold of 8, while the Corvina warehouse holds 140. The store manager, Lorcan Oyelaran-Shaw, gets an in-app alert. It shows both counts next to a Request transfer button. A transfer refills the shelf without a new purchase order.
fields.tab_content_4:
After 4 hours with no answer, the operations lead hears

Ezinne Fairweather-Kim gets a beeswax candle alert at 9:00 a.m., with 7 tins left against a threshold of 20. Nobody has marked it ordered by 1:00 p.m. At that point the app emails the operations lead, Saoirse Holloway-Adeyemi, with the item, the 9:00 a.m. alert time, and an Open alert button.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Low Stock Alert
fields.howto_description: These 7 steps set a low stock alert threshold for each item from real sales and give every alert an owner.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List the items that cannot run out
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pull 90 days of sales per item
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Set each threshold from the math
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Check the counts against the shelf
fields.howto_step_1_des: Start with the items that would lose you a sale or a regular customer if the shelf went empty. Write one owner next to each before you set any number, because an alert nobody owns gets read by nobody.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Export 90 days of sales for each item on the list and work out units sold per day. Note the supplier's lead time beside it, counted from the day you order to the day stock is on the shelf.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Multiply daily sales by the lead time in days, then add a buffer for late deliveries. A teapot that sells 2 a day, with a 5-day lead time and 2 days of buffer, gets a threshold of 14.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Connect the system that holds your counts, then pick 5 items and count them by hand. If a shelf count and the app's count disagree, fix the source before any alert goes out.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Run last month's sales through the rules and list every alert that would have fired. Compare that list with the stockouts you had, then change each threshold that missed with a prompt.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Switch on the critical items first
fields.howto_step_6_des: Turn on alerts for the items from step 1 only, and watch them for 2 weeks. Add the rest of the catalog once each owner says the alerts arrive with enough time to act.
fields.howto_step_7_des: Each quarter, pull up every alert that came too late to prevent a stockout and every one that fired weeks early. Raise or lower those thresholds, and adjust items whose sales shift with the season.

faq_plan.a: A low stock alert tells you when an item's on-hand quantity falls to or below the safety stock level you set, giving you time to reorder before you run out. The useful part is who receives it: one person who can act on that item that day.

faq_plan.q: How do I set up low stock alert?
faq_plan.a: Describe the rule in a prompt to Emergent's AI automation builder: the item and its threshold, plus the person who hears about it. Emergent builds the app and its logic from that description. Link your point of sale or online store through its API, and switch the alert on once a replay of last month matches what you saw on the shelf.

faq_plan.q: Should a low stock alert fire again on every sale below the threshold?
faq_plan.hint: How to automate low stock alerts?
faq_plan.a: No. Have it fire once when the count crosses the threshold, then stay quiet until someone marks the item ordered or a delivery lifts the count back above the line. An alert that repeats on every sale buries the one that mattered.

faq_plan.q: Can a low stock alert send a reorder request to the supplier?
faq_plan.hint: How to automate low stock alerts and reorder notifications?
faq_plan.a: Yes, but keep a person between the alert and the supplier. The app can draft the request with the item and a suggested quantity, and the buyer approves it before anything goes out. That approve-before-send step is the same one proposal automation puts in front of a quote.

faq_plan.q: Which items need an instant low stock alert instead of a daily summary?
faq_plan.hint: How to set up low-stock alerts for critical items?
faq_plan.a: Items that sell out within their supplier's lead time, and items a regular customer comes in for by name. Everything else can wait for one summary email at the start of the day. One list at 8:00 a.m. is easier to work through than 30 pings spread across a shift.

faq_plan.q: Should each store location get its own low stock alert threshold?
faq_plan.hint: How to set up automated low-stock alerts across multiple locations?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Base each store's number on that store's own sales, since two stores can sell the same item at different speeds. Give the warehouse a separate threshold too, set by supplier lead time, not shelf space. In an app built on Emergent, the counts for every location live in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: Who should receive low stock alerts at a business with several stores?
faq_plan.a: The person who can fix the shortage that day: the buyer for items that need a new order, the store manager for items another location can transfer. Name one person per item, plus a backup for vacations. If store managers start ignoring alerts, add a question about them to your next leadership survey and ask which ones they act on.

faq_plan.q: How can a low stock alert account for stock that is already on order?
faq_plan.a: Compare the threshold with units on hand plus units on open orders due before the shelf would empty. Without that, the alert fires again the day after the buyer orders. When the delivery arrives, the app moves those units from on order to on hand, and the item's alert resets.

faq_plan.q: What should a low stock alert message include?
faq_plan.a: Enough to act without opening another screen: the item, the count, the threshold, days of cover, the supplier, and one button such as Mark ordered. Leave out anything the owner would not use to decide. Emergent builds the alert and a live dashboard of open alerts from a plain-English prompt, and a new prompt changes any of them.

faq_plan.q: How do I know if my low stock alert thresholds are too high or too low?
faq_plan.a: Count two things each month: stockouts that happened even though an alert fired, and alerts that sat more than 2 weeks before anyone ordered. The first group needs higher thresholds; the second, lower ones. Then ask each alert owner to rate the timing on a short likert questionnaire, from far too early to far too late.

plan.angle: The top results for low stock alert are help-center pages for single inventory tools and one ecommerce app listing, each explaining a toggle inside its own product. This page shows the alert as a rule a shop owns: a fixed threshold per item, a threshold set by sales speed against supplier lead time, separate counts per store, and an escalation when nobody acts. All four run at one home goods retailer, Corvina Home Goods, as screens an operator can copy. Reordering itself belongs to the inventory management page; this page stays on who hears about low stock, when, and what they do next.

intent.evidence: Four alert types (item thresholds, sales speed vs lead time, store counts, escalation), a 7-step how-to with threshold math ('2 a day, with a 5-day lead time and 2 days of buffer, gets a threshold of 14'), a vendor table and a definition FAQ.

specificity.evidence: Buyer vocabulary throughout: 'days of cover', 'supplier's lead time', 'units on open orders', 'Request transfer'; table column 'Prompt for the workflow and the app around it'.

openers.evidence: Every feature and tab opens on a full sentence: 'Type the rule as you would tell a new buyer', 'Linen napkin sets sell 6 a day at Corvina Home Goods'.

craft.evidence: Two ', so' endings (feature_2, feature_4), under the limit; sentences short and single-idea.

voice.evidence: Concrete and unglamorous: 'the 1.2-liter pour-over kettle', '7 tins left against a threshold of 20'. Three forced link sentences in the FAQ are recorded as notes.

truth.evidence: Definition matches the boxhero.io quoted span ('falls to or below the safety stock level you set'); claims map to approved ids (alerts, realtime, no-caps, code-export, free-start); math checks: 54/6 = 9 days vs 10-day lead time, 6x2+... step 3 2x5+2x2 = 14, 9:00 to 1:00 p.m. = 4 hours.

distinct.evidence: Own story set at Corvina Home Goods (kettle, napkins, mugs, candles); no sibling primary in headings.
